en: Śrī Yogayājñavalkya. Edited by Śrī Prahlād Divāṇjī, 1954.
Transcribed by Jason Birch.
The First Chapter.
1.1ab: To Yājñavalkya, the best of sages, the omniscient one, stainless with knowledge; 1.1cd: the knower of the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures, who is ever devoted to meditation.
One who knows the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, who is firmly established in yogic practices,
who has conquered the senses, conquered anger, conquered [the desire for] food, and overcome disease; who is ascetic, has conquered enemies, is devoted to Brahman, and is dear to the Brahmins.
He had gone to the penance grove; he was gentle, devoted to the twilight worship,
surrounded by highly fortunate Brahmins who were knowers of Brahman,
equal toward all beings, peaceful, true to his word, and free from weariness.
1.5ab [He was] one who recognized virtue in all beings, whose sole purpose was the welfare of others;
1.5cd he spoke of himself as the Supreme Self to the sages of fierce splendor. 1.6ab To him, thus endowed with such qualities, the bride, the most excellent of women, [spoke].
The highly fortunate Maitreyī and Gārgī, the most eminent among the knowers of Brahman,
were present there; and having prostrated herself like a staff upon the ground before these sages of fierce splendor who were seated in the midst of the assembly, Gārgī spoke these words.
Gārgya said: "O Blessed One, knower of all scriptures, devoted to the welfare of all beings,
tell me the essence of yoga, together with its limbs and sub-limbs, according to the prescribed rule."
1.9ab Thus questioned by that woman in the midst of the assembly, the Blessed One,
looking at the sages with his eyes, spoke these words.
Yājñavalkya said:
1.10ab Arise, arise! May it be well with you, O Gārgī, best among the knowers of Brahman.
1.10cd I shall declare the entire essence of Yoga, as proclaimed by Brahmā in the past.
1.11ab With a concentrated mind, O Gārgī, listen to me as I speak.
Having spoken thus, Yājñavalkya— the foremost among the knowers of Brahman and a treasury of austerity—
[meditated upon] Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World, who dwells in the hearts of all beings,
Vāsudeva, the source of the universe, the object of meditation for yogis, and the stainless one.
Meditating in his heart with a well-composed mind upon Hṛṣīkeśa— the Lord, the Supreme Self, eternal, immortal, and blissful—
he gazed at her with both eyes and spoke these words out of compassion.
"Come, come, O Gārgī, you who are all-knowing and proficient in all the scriptures!
I shall duly declare to you the Yoga taught by the Creator, the Supreme Lord.
O sages, listen with concentrated minds along with Gārgī."
1.16ab Seated upon the lotus posture, the four-faced, immutable one;
1.16cd Brahmā, the supreme lord and creator of all things moving and unmoving.
1.17ab Once, having gone there, I praised him with hymns and bowed down before him.
1.17cd You have asked this very same matter that you now question me about.
1.18ab O God of gods, Lord of the world, four-faced Grandfather!
1.18cd Tell me by what action I may attain nirvāṇa, the imperishable liberation.
"O Lord, tell me truly that supreme and most secret knowledge.
Thus addressed by me, the self-existent Druhiṇa, the leader of the worlds,
looked at me with a gracious soul and spoke of the knowledges and actions.
1.20cd Two paths for knowledge are to be known as enjoined by the Veda;
1.21ab these two, which impel and restrain, are practiced by the wise.
1.21cd Whatever action prescribed for the castes and stages of life is preceded by desire and intention, [that leads to rebirth].
1.22ab This [action] would be "instigating" (pravartaka) and have rebirth as its cause;
1.22cd action enjoined by injunction as "it ought to be done," when devoid of desire, [is such].
1.23ab That by which something is performed correctly, being joined with knowledge, is "liberating" (nivartaka).
For that which causes cessation indeed turns a person away from rebirth;
for that which causes engagement everywhere is the cause of returning again.
It is precisely the action prescribed for the castes and stages of life, enjoined by the injunctions, and performed free from desire.
1.25ab For him who performs [his duty] according to the rules, O Gārgī, liberation is held in the palm of his hand.
1.25cd But for one who performs the very same action prescribed for his caste and stage of life out of desire,
1.26ab for him, by that act, dwelling in a womb is held in the palm of his hand.

Therefore, those who fear saṃsāra should perform the action prescribed by the injunctions, free from desire, always in accordance with the rules and accompanied by knowledge. And human beings born in the three worlds [should act] in accordance with the natural order.
1.28ab Thus, they likewise owe debts to the gods, the sages, and the ancestors.
1.28cd [One should discharge the debt] to the sages through celibate studentship, and to the ancestors through offspring.
1.29ab One should discharge the debt to the gods through sacrifice, practicing the dharma of one's own stage of life (āśrama).
1.29cd Four stages of life (āśramas) have been prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa, as enjoined by the Śruti.
1.30ab Three are prescribed for the Kṣatriya, and two or one for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra respectively.
1.30cd Having studied the Veda and the meaning of the Veda, along with its limbs (aṅgas) and sub-limbs (upāṅgas), according to the rule;

1.31ab He should bathe according to the path prescribed by the rules, observing the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya). 1.31cd Thereafter, he should procreate a son upon a consecrated woman of the same caste (savarṇā).
1.32ab He should perform sacrifices in the fire according to the rule, either together with his wife or without her.
1.32cd In a lonely region in the wilderness, provided with fruits, roots, and water,

1.33ab he should dwell constantly performing austerities, maintaining the *agnihotra* fire and remaining composed. 1.33cd Having internalized the fires within himself, he should then renounce according to the prescribed rule.
1.34ab Engaged in the stage of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa-āśrama*), constantly performing his obligatory duties (*nitya-karma*),

1.34cd he should worship the Self within himself for as long as he remains a "possessor of a field" (*kṣetrin*). 1.35ab And a Kṣatriya should likewise always practice in this manner until he reaches the stage of renunciation.
1.35cd Thus, a Vaiśya, being composed, should practice [the duties] starting from the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha).
1.36ab A Śūdra should always practice the householder’s stage (gṛhasthāśrama) through service. 1.36cd Celibacy (brahmacarya) for the Śūdra is also desired by some sages.
1.37ab For those born of marriages in the natural order, there are three stages of life (āśramas) for each of the three [higher castes].
1.37cd The conduct of those born of Śūdras is declared by the wise to be like that of the Śūdras. 1.38ab For those residing in the four stages of life, it must be performed daily, every single day.
1.38cd One should perform the action prescribed by injunction, free from desire and mental constructs.
1.39ab Therefore, O Lord of Yogins, you too should practice the dharma of your own stage of life (āśrama).
1.39cd With faith and according to the rules, properly perform both knowledge and action.
"Thus, the entire essence of my ritual action and its true nature as yoga have been taught to you. Having spoken thus, Brahmā himself then became established in yoga.
Hearing these words spoken by Yājñavalkya, Gārgī was filled with joy.
1.41cd Again, the fair-faced woman spoke once more to the best of sages in the midst of the rishis;
Gārgī said: 1.42ab "O Lord of Yogins, for one who performs the action prescribed by the injunctions together with knowledge..."
1.42cd "You have said that liberation exists; O Lord, tell us the knowledge regarding those two.
1.43ab Thus addressed by his wife, Yājñavalkya, a treasure-house of asceticism, 1.43cd gazed upon her with compassion and spoke the very form of knowledge.
Yājñavalkya said:
"Know that knowledge consists of yoga, and yoga is endowed with eight limbs. The union of the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) is called yoga."
1.45ab I shall explain the limbs [of yoga] to you correctly, just as I heard them before.
1.45cd O Gārgī, listen together with the sages with a concentrated mind.
1.46ab Restraint (yama) and observance (niyama), and likewise posture (āsana).

1.46cd Likewise, O Gārgī, breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and concentration (dhāraṇā); 1.47ab meditation (dhyāna) and absorption (samādhi)—these, O fair-faced one, are the limbs of yoga. 1.47cd Restraint (yama) and observance (niyama) are proclaimed to be tenfold.

1.48ab There are eight excellent postures; among them, three are the most excellent. 1.48cd Breath control (prāṇāyāma) is said to be of three kinds, and withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) is of five kinds.
1.49ab Retention (dhāraṇā) is said to be of five kinds, and meditation (dhyāna) is proclaimed to be of six kinds.
Among these, three are declared to be the highest; however, *samādhi* is of a single form.
Some maintain that there are many [yamas]; hear them in detail and individually:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion, and uprightness.

1.51ab Forbearance, fortitude, moderation in diet, and purity— these are the ten *yamas*. 1.51cd–1.52ab Not causing distress through action, mind, or speech toward any living being at any time is declared by the yogis to be non-violence (*ahiṃsā*).

1.52cd If non-violence were merely that which is enjoined by ritual injunction, it would result only in the production of affliction for living beings. 1.53ab For even though it is spoken of in the Veda, there is violence in rites such as *abhicāra* (malevolent magic). 1.53cd Truth is said to be what is beneficial to living beings, not merely the speaking of things as they are.
1.54ab–cd: To be without longing for the property of others by deed, thought, or word—this is called non-stealing (asteya) by the seers who perceive the truth. 1.55ab:
[This applies] at all times and in all circumstances, by deed, thought, or word.
1.55cd They declare that celibacy (*brahmacarya*) consists in the total renunciation of sexual intercourse.

1.56ab Celibacy belongs to those established in the stage of studentship (*brahmacaryāśrama*), to ascetics (*yatins*), and to those who have reached the final goal (*naiṣṭhika*). 1.56cd Celibacy is likewise prescribed for those who dwell in the forest (*āraṇyavāsins*).
1.57ab Sexual union with one’s own wife according to the prescribed rule during each fertile season,

1.57cd is declared to be the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for those dwelling in the householder stage of life. 1.58ab And this very celibacy is proclaimed as the duty even for a king who is a householder.

1.58cd Some wise men maintain that for Vaiśyas who follow their proper conduct, [the vow] is likewise [celibacy]. 1.59ab But for a Śūdra, it is proclaimed that his celibacy consists solely in service. 1.59cd Or rather, constant service to the Guru is declared to be his celibacy.
1.60ab For all four [classes], five elders are enjoined by the Veda:
1.60cd Mother, father, teacher, maternal uncle, and likewise the father-in-law.
1.61ab Among these, women are declared to be the foremost, as are the teacher and the parents.

Among these, however, one is the preeminent teacher, a knower of the ultimate truth (1.61cd). One should constantly honor that most excellent knower of Brahman, who is devoted to his obligatory duties, through service, by which means the Guru becomes satisfied (1.62).

1.63 Compassion toward all living beings is traditionally defined as universal benevolence; 1.63–64 uprightness is the uniformity of one's mental, vocal, and physical actions whether engaged in those duties prescribed by law or in their opposites.
1.64cd That state of equanimity which embodied beings maintain toward all things, whether pleasant or unpleasant,
1.65ab is declared by the learned who proclaim the Vedas to be patience (kṣamā),
even when there is loss of wealth or separation from kinsmen and prosperity.
1.66ab And when those two are attained, the steadying of the mind everywhere is fortitude (dhṛti).
1.66cd Eight mouthfuls are to be eaten by a sage; sixteen by forest-dwellers;
1.67ab Thirty-two by householders; and as much as desired by students of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin).
1.67cd For among these, this [practice] consists of moderate eating, whereas for others it is eating little. 1.68ab Purity is said to be of two kinds: external and likewise internal.
1.68cd External purity is traditionally held to consist of earth and water, while internal purity is the purification of the mind.
1.69ab And the purification of the mind is to be understood through dharma and the science of the inner self (adhyātmavidyā).
1.69cd O sinless one, both the science of the self and dharma were obtained by me from my father and my teacher.
1.70ab Therefore, at all times, all those who seek liberation should rely upon them.
1.70cd: "The gurus, endowed with sacred learning, are to be honored through speech, mind, and other means.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Śrī Yogayājñavalkya. 2.1ab:
"Austerity, contentment, faith in the scriptures, charity, and worship of the Lord..."
2.1cd And listening to the established doctrine, as well as modesty, discernment, recitation, and vows;
2.2ab These are declared to be the observances (niyamas); hear all of them individually.
2.2cd By the path prescribed by rule, through such penances as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*.

2.3ab Ascetics say that the supreme austerity is the withering of the body. 2.3cd [They hold this] so that a person may always be content with whatever is obtained by chance. 2.4ab That state of mind which consists of such contentment, the seers declare to be the characteristic of happiness.
2.4cd Faith in what is righteous and what is unrighteous is called *āstikya* (theistic conviction).

2.5ab Wealth acquired through just means, as well as food or anything else that is given, 2.5cd when bestowed upon those who ask with a spirit of faith— this is declared to be *dāna* (charitable giving).
2.6ab–cd: Worshiping Viṣṇu or even another deity with devotion, according to one's ability and with a serene disposition—this indeed is the worship of the Lord. 2.7ab:
A heart free from passion and the like, and speech that is not corrupted by falsehood and so forth.
2.7cd A body free from violence and other such acts—this is the worship of the Lord.
2.8ab Listening to the established doctrine (siddhānta) is declared by the wise to be the listening to the Vedānta.
2.8cd For a kṣatriya, as for a twice-born, listening to the established doctrine is thus prescribed by the wise.
2.9ab Some authorities maintain that [the hearing of the scriptures] is intended for the Vaiśyas who are virtuous and of good conduct,

2.9cd as well as for Śūdras, women, and ascetics established in their own duties. 2.10ab The learned have declared that listening to the Purāṇas constitutes the hearing of the established doctrine (siddhānta).

2.10cd Whatever action may be contemptible within the paths of the Vedas or the world, 2.11ab the sense of shame one feels toward that is proclaimed to be *hrī* (modesty). 2.11cd And the faith one has in all prescribed duties is what constitutes *mati* (discernment).
2.12ab Even when instructed by a guru, [one must remain] avoiding that which is outside the Vedas. 2.12cd The practice of mantras according to the path prescribed by rule is known as *japa*.
2.13ab Having studied the Veda, or the Sūtra, or the Purāṇa together with the Itihāsas...
2.13cd And that which is the practice of these is known as *japa*, which is repetition.
2.14ab *Japa* is declared to be of two kinds: vocal (*vācika*) and likewise mental (*mānasa*).
2.14cd Vocal [recitation] is proclaimed to be of two kinds: whispered (*upāṃśu*) and loud (*uccais*).
2.15ab The mental [recitation] is established as being of two kinds, through the distinction between thinking and meditating.
2.15cd It is said that the whispered [recitation] is a thousand times more effective than the loud recitation.
2.16ab And the mental [recitation] is said to be a thousand times more effective than the whispered one.
2.16cd And likewise, meditative concentration (dhyāna) is said to be a thousand times more effective than mental recitation.
2.17ab However, loud recitation yields the aforementioned fruit for all [methods], provided it is not heard by others; 2.17cd if it is heard, even that becomes fruitless.
2.18ab Meditating always upon the seer, the meter, the presiding deity,
and the mantra, 2.18cd that alone, O Gārgī, is the recitation of the mantra that bestows fruit.
2.19ab [It should be performed] as previously instructed by a gracious guru, with his permission.
2.19cd: "The vow is the adoption of means for the sake of dharma and for the sake of self-perfection.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Śrī-Yogayājñavalkya*.
Yājñavalkya said:
3.1ab Now I shall describe the postures; listen, O Gārgī, rich in ascetic merit!
3.1cd Svastika, Gomukha, Padma, Vīra, and likewise Siṃhāsana;
3.2ab Bhadra, Muktāsana, and indeed Mayūrāsana as well.
3.2cd Likewise, O lady of excellent hips, I shall describe their individual characteristics separately.
3.3ab Having placed both soles of the feet properly between the knees and the thighs, 3.3cd sitting comfortably with the body straight— this they call *svastika*.
3.4ab Having placed the two ankles at the sides of one's own body's seam, 3.4cd placing the right ankle on the left [thigh] and the other [left ankle] on the right;
3.5ab this is declared to be the *svastika* posture, which destroys all sins.
3.5cd One should place the right ankle on the left side of the back;
3.6ab likewise, one should place the left [ankle] on the right side, so that it forms the cow’s mouth (gomukha). 3.6cd And one should bind the two big toes with the hands in reverse order.
3.7ab O best of Brahmins, having placed both soles of the feet upon the thighs,
3.7cd this becomes the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), which is honored by all. 3.8ab Then, placing one foot resting upon one thigh, [the other is likewise positioned].
3.8cd In the other [posture], the thighs are likewise described as being in the *vīrāsana* position. 3.9ab One should place the two ankles below the scrotum, on either side of the perineal seam.
3.9cd The right [ankle] with the left ankle, and likewise the other with the right.

3.10ab Having placed both hands upon the knees and having extended the fingers of one's own hands, 3.10cd With mouth wide open, one should gaze at the tip of the nose, being well-composed. 3.11ab This shall be the lion-throne (siṃhāsana), always honored by yogins.
3.11cd One should place the two ankles below the scrotum and on either side of the perineal seam.
3.12ab Having firmly bound the sides and feet with the hands so that they are perfectly motionless,
3.12cd this shall be the Bhadrāsana posture, which removes all diseases and poisons.
3.13ab Pressing the delicate *sīvanī* [seam] on the left side with the left ankle,
3.13cd and the left [side] with the right ankle— this is declared to be *muktāsana*.
3.14ab Likewise, having placed the left ankle above the penis, and likewise above that...
Having placed the space between the ankles [on the ground], this is indeed the *muktāsana*; or else,
having firmly supported the earth with the palms of both hands,
one should place the elbows of the two hands at the sides of the navel.
3.16ab With the head and feet raised high, standing in the sky like a staff—
3.16cd this is the Peacock Posture (mayūrāsana), which destroys all sins.
3.17ab All internal diseases and poisons are likewise destroyed.

3.17cd–18ab: "Well-joined with the restraints (yama), the observances (niyama), and the postures (āsana), and having performed the purification of the channels (nāḍīśuddhi), one should then practice breath control (prāṇāyāma). Thus ends the third chapter of the Śrī Yogayājñavalkya.
The Fourth Chapter.
4.1ab Having heard this speech of the wise Yājñavalkya,
4.1cd the illustrious female ascetic spoke again in the midst of the assembly.
Gārgya said:
"O Blessed One, O Master, tell me according to the prescribed rule how the purification of the channels is performed;
by what means do the channels of all embodied beings become purified?"
4.3ab Furthermore, [tell me] the origin of the channels and their movement according to the rule;
4.3cd what kind of bulb (kanda) is said to exist, and how many vital winds (vāyu) reside there?
4.4ab Also, the locations of the winds and their respective functions individually.
"O best among those who bear bodies, you ought to explain all those things that are to be known within this body; for there is no knower of them other than you.
Thus addressed by his wife, he, with his mind fully intent upon that matter, [spoke].
4.6ab Having gazed intently at Gārgī, Yājñavalkya spoke all of that: 4.6cd "The body, indeed, consists of ninety-six finger-breadths."
4.7ab Know this, O beloved, that for all living beings, [the life-force] is measured by one's own fingers; 4.7cd the vital breath (prāṇa) extends twelve finger-breadths beyond the body.
4.8ab Some of the best of sages say it is fourteen finger-breadths.
4.8cd Wise men declare that it is exactly twelve finger-breadths [in length].

4.9ab The wise man, by means of the practice of yoga, should make the wind situated within himself equal to or even less than the fire situated within himself. 4.9cd [He should do so] through the practice of yoga.
4.10ab He alone is the supreme knower of Brahman; he is the most excellent of men and worthy of worship.
4.10cd O best of the twice-born, by means of the fire residing within yourself, born of yoga, 4.11ab conquer the vital breath (mātariśvan) abiding within yourself through the practice of yoga.
4.11cd Within the center of the body is the seat of fire, possessing the luster of molten gold.
4.12ab For humans it is triangular, and for quadrupeds it is square;
4.12cd for winged creatures it is circular—this truth I declare to you.
4.13ab But in the middle of that, the slender flame of fire always remains. 4.13cd If you wish to hear where the center of the body is, listen:
4.14ab It is two finger-breadths above the anus and two finger-breadths below the penis.
4.14cd The middle of the body is said to be the center between those two for human beings. 4.15ab For quadrupeds, however, it is the middle of the heart; for animals, the middle of the belly.
4.15cd But for birds, O beautiful lady, it is said to be the middle of the belly.
4.16ab For humans, the location of the *kanda* is nine finger-breadths from the center of the body.
4.16cd Its height and its length are likewise four finger-breadths.
4.17ab Its shape is like that of an egg, adorned with the skin and other [layers].
4.17cd For quadrupeds, animals, and birds, [the vital point] is in the middle of the belly.
4.18ab That middle is called the navel; in the navel, the wheel originates.
4.18cd It is endowed with twelve spokes, and by means of it, the body is supported.
4.19ab Driven by sin and merit, the individual soul (*jīva*) revolves within this wheel. 4.19cd It revolves like a spider situated in the midst of a web of threads.
4.20ab Within this root-wheel of the soul, this vital breath (*prāṇa*) moves below.
4.20cd The individual soul (jīva), mounted upon the vital breath (prāṇa), is always present within all beings.
4.21ab Above that is the location of Kuṇḍalinī, situated transversely and upwards from the navel.
4.21cd She consists of the eightfold primordial nature (aṣṭaprakṛti) and is coiled eight times.
4.22ab Having properly restrained the movement of the vital breaths and the constant flow of water, food, and so forth,
4.22cd she remains forever situated, having completely blocked [the channels] on all sides around the bulb (kanda).
4.23ab Likewise, she completely envelops the opening of the Brahma-randhra with her own mouth.
4.23cd But at the time of yoga, she is awakened by the apāna together with the fire.
4.24ab Throbbing in the space of the heart, in the form of a serpent, intensely radiant;
4.24cd the wind then proceeds through the suṣumṇā by means of its own companion, the wind.
4.25ab The channel situated in the middle of the *kanda* is celebrated as the *suṣumṇā*.
4.25cd All those known as channels (*nāḍī*) reside all around this wheel (*cakra*).
4.26ab Among all these channels, however, these fourteen are the principal ones.
4.26cd Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Suṣumnā, and Sarasvatī;
4.27ab Vāruṇī, Pūṣā, Hastijihvā, and Yaśasvinī; 4.27cd Viśvodarā, Kuhū, Śaṅkhinī, and Payasvinī.
4.28ab Alambuṣā, Gāndhārī, and these fourteen principal ones;
4.28cd among them, three are the most principal, and among those three, one is the highest of the high.
4.29ab That is called Suṣumnā, the path to liberation, the sustainer of the universe.
4.29cd O Gārgī, the Suṣumnā is well-established in the center of the bulb (kanda).
4.30ab That channel (nāḍī) situated in the middle of the back is indeed established in the head.
4.30cd That Suṣumnā is the path to liberation; it is celebrated as the Brahma-randhra.
4.31ab That very [power] is to be known as unmanifest; she is indeed remembered as the subtle Vaiṣṇavī. 4.31cd Iḍā and Piṅgalā are her left and right [channels].
4.32ab Iḍā is situated on her left, and Piṅgalā is situated on the right.
4.32cd The moon and the sun move within the *iḍā* and the *piṅgalā*.
4.33ab The moon is to be known as being in the *iḍā*, and the sun is traditionally said to be in the *piṅgalā*.
4.33cd The moon is said to be of the nature of *tamas*, while the sun is said to be of the nature of *rajas*.
The portion of the sun is the poison-portion; the portion of the moon is known as nectar.
These two sustain the entirety of time, consisting of night and day.
Suṣumnā is the consumer of that time; this is declared to be the secret.
Sarasvatī and Kuhu are situated on the two sides of Suṣumṇā;
Gāndhārī and Hastijihvā are on the back and side of Iḍā;
and Viśvodarā is situated between Kuhu and Hastijihvā.
4.37ab Between Yaśasvinī and Kuhū stands Vāruṇī;
4.37cd Between Pūṣā and Sarasvatī stands Payasvinī. 4.38ab Between Gāndhārī and Sarasvatī stands Śaṅkhinī.
4.38cd And Alambuṣā, O best of Brahmins, is situated below the center of the *kanda*. 4.39ab Kuhū is situated in the eastern part of the *suṣumṇā*, extending as far as the genitals.
4.39cd Vāruṇī, which moves everywhere, is both below and above the *kuṇḍalī*.
4.40ab Yaśasvinī is held to extend from the southern [channel] to the big toe.
4.40cd Know, O my beloved, that Piṅgalā, moving upward in the south, reaches to the nose.
4.41ab And Pūṣā in the south reaches to the eye, situated behind Piṅgalā.
Likewise, O Gārgī, the Payasvinī is held to extend as far as the right ear; the Sarasvatī is established above, reaching up to the tongue;
and the Śaṅkhinī, O best of Brahmins, is considered to rise upward from the left ear.
4.43ab Gāndhārī is situated behind the left eye at the back of the iḍā.
4.43cd And the iḍā is established on the left side, extending to the end of the left nostril.
4.44ab Likewise, Hastijihvā is held to extend to the end of the big toe of the left foot.
4.44cd But the channel called Viśvodarā is situated in the middle of the belly.
4.45ab O highly fortunate one, Alambuṣā extends downward from the root of the anus.
4.45cd These others have arisen, as well as other vessels within them.
4.46ab Just as [the veins] are on the leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, so too are they on the petals of the lotus;
4.46cd all these channels (*nāḍī*) are to be understood in this way, O you whose wealth is austerity.
4.47ab Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna—these are the vital breaths.
4.47cd Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya—
4.48ab these ten winds move through all the channels (nāḍīs).
4.48cd Among these, the five winds beginning with Prāṇa are known as the primary ones.
Among these, these two—prāṇa and apāna—are the most principal in the best of men;
of these two, prāṇa alone is always the primary one for all living beings.
It resides in the middle of the mouth and nose, in the center of the heart, and in the middle of the navel.
4.50cd Some say that the abode of the vital breath (prāṇa) is even in the big toe.
4.51ab–cd The one known as prāṇa, encircling the kuṇḍalī both below and above,
shines forth like a lamp when it is fixed within these four.
4.52ab Some say that the abode of the apāna wind is in the anus, penis, thighs, and knees; 4.52cd others indeed say it is in the abdomen, testicles, hips, shanks, and navel.
4.53ab The apāna wind stands between the anus and the fire-chamber (the stomach).
4.53cd–54ab: And it illuminates both below and above, like a lamp, along with the *kuṇḍalī*.
4.54cd: *Vyāna* resides in the ears, the eyes, the middle of the neck, the ankles, the nose, the throat, and the region of the buttocks; of this there is no doubt.
4.55ab The udāna wind resides in all the joints, as well as in the feet and hands.

4.55cd The samāna wind is situated pervading all the limbs, having spread throughout the entire body. 4.56ab It distributes all the consumed flavors throughout the body together with the digestive fire (vahni).
4.56cd It moves through the seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍī*).

4.57ab Only the single *samāna* wind remains, pervading and abiding together with the fire. (Better as in the *Matsya Purāṇa*: "Only this *samāna* wind remains, pervading and abiding in this body. 4.57cd Together with the fires, it is present everywhere throughout the body, including its limbs and sub-limbs.

The five winds, beginning with *nāga*, are situated within [the body] at the locations of Agastya and the other [vital points]. The water, food, and juices located in the stomach are brought into equilibrium;
then the *prāṇa* wind, residing in the center of the stomach, separates them one by one.

4.59cd–4.60ab: Again, having placed water upon the fire and food and other substances upon the water, the downward-moving breath (apāna) itself reaches that [water], and together with that very breath, the wind blows again toward the fire located within the center of the body.
4.60cd: [It] blows there toward the fire situated in the middle of the body.
4.61ab Fanned by the wind, the fire [is ignited] by the apāna breath very gradually; 4.61cd then it blazes, O best of Brahmins, within one's own body in the center of the family [of elements].
4.62ab Thereupon, the fire blazes with flames, impelled by the prāṇa breath.
4.62cd Then the water, having entered the interior of the stomach, became excessively hot.
4.63ab The food, together with its condiments, was placed upon the water. 4.63cd Thereupon, the digestive fire thoroughly cooked it by means of the heated water.
4.64ab Sweat and urine would be water; the nutrient essence (*rasa*) would take the form of semen.
4.64cd Feces would be food, O Gārgī; Prāṇa would perform these functions individually. 4.65ab Together with the Samāna wind, it [Prāṇa] distributes the nutrient essence throughout all the channels.

4.65cd Pervading [the body] in the form of breath, the vital air (māruta) moves within the body. 4.66ab Through the nine apertures of space, all the winds continuously perform the excretion of feces, urine, and so forth within bodies.
4.67ab Exhalation, inhalation, and coughing are proclaimed as the function of *prāṇa*.

4.67cd This—namely, the evacuation of feces, urine, and so forth—is the function of the *apāna* wind. 4.68ab The effort involved in rejection, appropriation, and so on, is considered to be the function of *vyāna*.
4.68cd That which consists of the lifting up of the body and so forth is declared to be the function of udāna.
4.69ab The nourishing of the body and so forth is proclaimed as the function of samāna.
4.69cd Furthermore, that quality which consists of belching and so forth is proclaimed as the function of nāga.
4.70ab The closing [of the eyes] and so forth belong to the tortoise (kūrma), and sneezing belongs to the *kṛkara*.
4.70cd O best of Brahmins, lassitude is proclaimed as the function of the *devadatta*.
4.71ab Swelling and all other such functions are proclaimed to belong to the *dhanañjaya*.
4.71cd Having thus understood the arrangement of the channels (nāḍī) and the locations and functions of the vital airs (vāyu),
4.72ab perform the purification of the channels according to the method prescribed by the rule.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Śrī Yogayājñavalkya*.
The Fifth Chapter.
Gārgya said:
"O Blessed One, most excellent among the knowers of Brahman, proficient in all the scriptures..."
"5.1cd By what means may my channels be purified? Tell me, O Lord.
5.2ab Thus addressed by the woman who speaks of Brahman, that Brāhmaṇa, a knower of Brahman, 5.2cd gazed upon her with compassion and explained the purification of the channels.
Yājñavalkya said: Engaged in actions prescribed by the injunctions, free from desire and mental resolve,
endowed with restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), and devoid of all [worldly] attachments.
5.4ab One who has acquired knowledge, who has conquered anger, and who is devoted to truth and dharma; 5.4cd who delights in service to his teachers and is devoted to his father and mother;
5.5ab who remains in his own stage of life, follows virtuous conduct, and is well-instructed by the learned.
5.5cd Having reached the penance grove, which was well-provided with fruits, roots, and water;
5.6ab there, in a delightful and pure place filled with the sound of Vedic recitation; 5.6cd surrounded by peaceful knowers of Brahman who were devoted to their own duties.
5.7ab And in a place well-filled with water and endowed with various kinds of flowers, 5.7cd and filled with fruits and roots, which grants the fruit of all desires;
5.8ab either in a temple, or by a river, or in a village, or else in a city.
Having constructed a very beautiful monastery (maṭha) endowed with all means of protection,
one who is constantly engaged in one's own duty and joined by bathing at the three times of day should practice yoga while listening to the Vedānta therein.
5.10 Some sages say that those who are devoted to austerity and sacred study,
who are intent on their own duty, peaceful, and always delighted in the tantras, [should practice] in a delightful, secluded dwelling, free from wind and sun.
5.11 [They should practice] in a beautiful, solitary abode, devoid of wind and heat.
5.11cd Being purified and composed, joined with the rites prescribed by the injunctions; 5.12ab the wise one, having always applied the mantras to his body and wearing white ashes,
5.12cd should then spread kusha grass upon a soft seat and over that an antelope skin.
Having thoroughly worshipped Vināyaka with fruits, roots, water, and other offerings,
and having bowed to one's chosen deity and the Guru, one should then ascend the seat; facing either east or north, one should personally take one's place, having mastered the posture.
With neck, head, and body held straight, with the mouth closed and perfectly motionless,
one should always fix the gaze correctly on the tip of the nose, placing the right hand upon the other;
[therein] the orb of the moon is at the tip of the nose, overspread with a network of moonlight.
5.16ab But the fourth letter of the seventh group, joined with the bindu,

5.16cd— seeing it dripping nectar with his eyes, being well-composed; 5.17ab— having drawn in the breath through the *iḍā* and filled it so that it remains in the belly (*iḍayā vāyum āpūrya kumbhayitvodarasthitam*).
5.17cd–18ab: Then, meditating on the fire situated in the center of the body, endowed with a garland of flames,
and meditating on the letter *ra* joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*) and established within the circle of fire,
one should subsequently exhale slowly through the *piṅgalā* channel.
5.19ab Again, the wise one, having filled the breath through the *piṅgalā* on the right side,
5.19cd the intelligent one should exhale again very slowly through the *iḍā*.
5.20ab Or for three or four years, or even for three or four months.
5.20cd One should practice this in secret six times daily during the three junctions of the day.
5.21ab One attains purification of the channels, characterized by distinct signs:
5.21cd lightness of the body and the radiance of the fire residing in the stomach.
5.22ab The manifestation of sound—these are the signs indicating its accomplishment.

Thus ends the fifth chapter in the venerable *Yogayājñavalkya*.
The Sixth Chapter.
Yājñavalkya said:
6.1ab Now, therefore, I shall explain breath control (prāṇāyāma) according to the prescribed rule.
6.1cd And you, O Gārgī of lovely countenance, listen with a concentrated mind.
6.2ab The union of the prāṇa and apāna breaths is declared to be prāṇāyāma.
6.2cd It is called prāṇāyāma by means of exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka).
6.3ab For these—exhalation, inhalation, and retention—are composed of the three *varṇas*.
6.3cd This is declared to be the *praṇava*, and the *prāṇāyāma* consists of that.
6.4ab Having drawn in the air through the *iḍā* and having filled it, [one holds] it situated within the belly.
6.4cd One should there recollect the syllable *A* slowly for sixteen measures (*mātrā*).
6.5ab Thereafter, one should retain the filled [breath] for sixty-four measures.
6.5cd Recollecting here as well the form of the syllable *U*, one should mutter the *praṇava*.
6.6ab Or, as long as it can be held, one should perform retention joined with *japa*. 6.6cd Afterwards, one should exhale the filled breath together with the external air.
6.7ab Again, O Gārgī, one should slowly [exhale] through the Piṅgalā for thirty-two *mātrās*.
Even while recollecting the form of the syllable *ma*, one should mutter the *praṇava*;
this constitutes *prāṇāyāma*, and one should practice it again in this same manner. Then, having filled [the breath] through the *piṅgalā* with sixteen *mātrās*.
6.9ab Here too, being well-composed and recollecting the form of the syllable *ukāra*,

6.9cd one should hold the breath (*prāṇa*) filled [within] for twice twenty [moments], while reciting the *praṇava*. 6.10ab Here, while recollecting the form known as the syllable *makāra*, one should mutter [the mantra] to Maheśvara.
6.10cd Or else, one should exhale the breath through the *iḍā* for as long as it can be managed;
6.11ab In this very same way, one should perform it again, filling [the breath] through the *iḍā* as before; 6.12ab [The breath] well-joined with the *praṇava* and combined with the *vyāhṛtis*.
6.12cd A brahmin should recite the Gāyatrī three times during each restraint of the breath.
6.13ab He should perform it again in this same manner three times, and likewise again at the three junctions of the day.
6.13cd Or else, he should constantly practice either a Vedic or a worldly [mantra].
6.14ab During the restraint of the breath (*prāṇāyāma*), the wise man should recite that [mantra] twenty times each.
6.14cd A Brahmin who is endowed with Vedic learning and always devoted to his own duty,
6.15ab should recite a Vedic mantra, and never a worldly one.
6.15cd Some desire worldly recitation for the sake of the welfare of living beings.
6.16ab The recitation during the restraint of breath (prāṇāyāma) prescribed for a Kṣatriya is said to be like that of a twice-born (Dvija).
6.16cd [It is also prescribed] for Vaiśyas endowed with dharma, and for women, Śūdras, and ascetics.

6.17ab O Gārgī, for the restraint of the vital breaths (prāṇa-saṃyamana), a mantra devoid of the syllable Om (praṇava) is desired by the wise; 6.17cd or else a Śiva-mantra ending with "namaḥ," or a Vaiṣṇava mantra. 6.18ab Or rather, a Śūdra should practice a worldly mantra according to the prescribed rule.
6.18cd A woman, during the restraint of breath (*prāṇāyāma*), should mutter that [mantra] twenty-twice.
6.19ab A Śūdra and women should never mutter Vedic [mantras].
6.19cd Some, however, desire that a Vaiśya who remains in his own stage of life (*āśrama*) may mutter the Vedic [mantras].

6.20ab At both twilights, a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas should always perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the Gāyatrī or with the syllable Om (praṇava). 6.20cd [He should do so] at both twilights, always. 6.21ab He should thus constantly perform sixteen breath controls.
6.21cd Even those who have killed an embryo are purified within a month by those [recitations] performed daily.
6.22ab After three seasons, they purify him from the sin committed in another life;
6.22cd After a year, the killer of a Brahmin becomes pure; therefore, one should practice this constantly.
6.23ab But those who are thus devoted to the practice of yoga and intent upon their own duty,
6.23cd indeed all become liberated by the very restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa).
6.24ab The filling of the air from the outside into the abdomen is indeed the *pūraka* [inhalation].
6.24cd Retention of breath like a full pitcher is known as *kumbhaka*.
6.25ab The expulsion of air from the abdomen to the outside is remembered as *recaka*.
6.25cd That which produces perspiration during the *prāṇāyāmas* is considered inferior.
6.26ab Trembling is said to be the middling stage, and rising is the highest.
6.26cd One should perform each preceding stage until the highest is attained.
6.27ab When the highest stage is achieved, O Gārgī, one becomes happy through breath control (prāṇāyāma).
6.27cd By that very [process], the vital breath dissolves; it is superior to the body.
6.28ab And by that, the body rises up, having assumed its seat. 6.28cd For it, inhalation and exhalation do not exist in any way whatsoever.

6.29ab Even if both those qualities were inherent in the body, 6.29cd nevertheless, they are destroyed by that supreme prāṇāyāma. 6.30ab Upon their destruction, one becomes capable of performing kevalakumbhaka.

6.30cd–31ab: Leaving aside exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka), the comfortable retention of breath (vāyu-dhāraṇa) is said to be this prāṇāyāma; it is indeed the kevala-kumbhaka (isolated retention). 6.31cd: That which one performs after exhaling and then inhaling is indeed the sahita-kumbhaka (retention with accompaniment).
6.32ab One should practice *kumbhaka* constantly, both with [recaka and pūraka] and then alone.
6.32cd One should practice the *sahita* [type] until the mastery of the *kevala* [type] is attained.
6.33ab When the *kevala* *kumbhaka*, which is devoid of exhalation and inhalation, has been mastered, [one is ready for the next stage].
6.33cd Nothing whatsoever is difficult for him to obtain within the three worlds.
6.34ab He attains swiftness like that of the mind, and graying hair and other such signs perish.
6.34cd This is the great path to liberation, belonging to the inner self known by the letter 'Ma'.
6.35ab This breath-restraint (kumbhaka), which is the control of the vital breath (prāṇa), also produces a sound.
6.35cd What is called "control of the vital breath" is the retention of the breath within the body.
6.36ab This is the means for conquering the vital breath, and it destroys all forms of death.

6.36cd I shall tell you, in accordance with reality, a certain means for mastering the vital breath (prāṇa). 6.37ab Having drawn the breath from the exterior and filled it so that it resides within the abdomen,
[one should hold it] with effort at the center of the navel, the tip of the nose, and the big toe.
6.38ab One should always restrain the vital breath (prāṇa) with the mind during the periods of the twilights (saṃdhyā).
6.38cd Liberated from all diseases and free from fatigue, the yogi shall live [long].
6.39ab O Gārgī, the restraint of the breath at the tip of the nose is the cause of victory over the winds.
6.39cd By fixing [the breath] in the center of the navel, there shall be the destruction of all diseases.
6.40ab By fixing it in the big toe, the body attains lightness.
6.40cd That man who, having drawn in the wind through the tongue, drinks it constantly, [attains success].
Fatigue and burning sensations do not afflict him, nor do diseases perish for him who,
during the twilights or at the time of Brahmā, draws in and drinks the air. O auspicious lady, after three months, Sarasvatī, the goddess of speech, arises within him.
6.42cd Through the practice of six months, one is liberated from great diseases.
6.43ab He who, having projected the self into the self, should maintain it within the *kuṇḍalī*;
6.43cd others know that for him, diseases such as consumption (*kṣaya*) and the like perish.
6.44ab Drawing in the wind with the tongue and obstructing it at the root of the tongue,
6.44cd the wise one who drinks the nectar attains every auspiciousness.
6.45ab Having drawn the self into the Self by means of the *iḍā* [channel] between the eyebrows,
6.45cd He who drinks the food of the thirty gods is liberated from diseases.
6.46ab Or, having directed the vital air through the two channels into the navel, the abdomen, or the sides; 6.46cd he who maintains it there for one *ghaṭikā* is completely freed from diseases.

6.47ab For one month, at the three junctions of the day, having drawn in the wind with the tongue, 6.47cd he who drinks it as a food for the thirty [gods] should retain it within the middle of the abdomen. 6.48ab Tumors, *aṣṭhīlā*, splenic disorders, and others likewise born from the three *doṣas* [are cured]. (Yogakalpalatā: "Tumor" refers to abdominal dropsy and splenic enlargement located in the middle of the abdomen.)
6.48cd All diseases situated in the middle of the abdomen are indeed destroyed for him. 6.49ab All fevers perish, as do various kinds of poisons.
6.49cd What is the use of saying more, O Gārgī? Even gray hair and other such ailments are destroyed.
6.50ab Thus, O fair-faced one, is the means for conquering the wind (vāyu) of the vital breath (prāṇa).
6.50cd Having assumed a posture and likewise with a concentrated mind,
6.51ab the wise man, having forcibly subdued the senses from their objects by restraining them, [should practice].
6.51cd Drawing the *apāna* upward with the *praṇava*, being fully concentrated; 6.52ab One should properly bind the sense organs, beginning with the ears, using both hands.
6.52cd [One should cover] both ears with the two thumbs and both eyes with the two index fingers.
Having covered the two nostrils with the middle fingers,
one should indeed hold [the breath] at the crown of the head for as long as the experience of bliss lasts;
by this very means, the vital breath departs, and thereafter it becomes a destroyer of life.
6.54cd In the *brahmarandhra*, within the *suṣumnā* like a thread inside a lotus stalk,
6.55ab the arising of the *nāda* occurs by this very [process], resembling pure crystal; 6.55cd the *nāda* extends up to the crown of the head, rising like the neck-pole of a lute.
6.56ab At first, it resembles the sound of a conch shell; in the middle, it is like the sound of clouds.
6.56cd When the resonance has entered the aperture of space, it is like a mountain torrent.
6.57ab When the wind has entered the aperture of space and the mind is firmly established in the Self, [the resonance arises].
6.57cd Then the embodied being becomes blissful, for by that means the vital air has been conquered.
6.58ab But other yogins here, who are even-minded, say:
6.58cd "Devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma) and purified, they are free from exhaling and inhaling."

6.59ab One should press the vein at the suture with the left ankle; 6.59cd [one should apply it] below the testicles, a fine [vein], and on the left side for the right [leg]. 6.60ab O Gārgī, one should bind it firmly and without gaps between the shank and the thigh.
With neck, head, and shoulders held straight, with back, belly, and hips even,
gazing at the right ankle with his eyes while standing upright,
he should utter the syllable *praṇava* together with his mind.
6.62ab A twice-born man, his mind focused on nothing else, always sits upon his seat in solitude;
6.62cd and so too the Kṣatriya, O lady of beautiful hips, while pronouncing the syllable *praṇava*.
6.63ab With his senses conquered, he sits upon his seat in solitude, his mind fixed on nothing else.
6.63cd Vaiśyas, Śūdras, women, and other men who are devoted to the practice of yoga,
6.64ab whether reciting the Śaiva, the Vaiṣṇava, or even another [scripture], 6.64cd sit upon their seat with undistracted minds, gazing at a lamp held in their hand.
6.65ab Life itself, which causes the destruction of life, has entered the family of fire by means of this [practice].
6.65cd One with undistracted mind should practice thus until victory over the smoke-bannered [fire] is attained.
6.66ab For one performing this retention, there shall be power regarding desired food.
[...of that... at the place of fire, one should [place] the wind. (6.66cd) Then the body attains lightness and the digestive fire increases.
(6.67ab) Therefore, having perceived the signs, one should mentally superimpose the wind upon it.
6.67cd While reciting the mantra, one should restrain [the breath] for a long duration in the center of the navel.
6.68ab As long as the mind does not dissolve into this solar orb at the navel,
6.68cd so long should the wise person practice, self-controlled and fixed in his posture.

6.69ab By this very concentration (dhāraṇā) situated in the center of the navel, the vital air (māruta) enters the Kuṇḍalinī, and the fire burns there; of this there is no doubt. 6.70ab There, heated by the fire and moved by itself through the wind, [the Kuṇḍalinī rises].
6.70cd Then, having extended the body of the serpent, it attains awakening. 6.71ab When this wheel-possessor (cakrin) at the base of the navel has awakened, it wanders;
6.71cd the one known as prāṇa then proceeds into the *suṣumṇā* at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
6.72 When that vital wind has entered the *suṣumṇā*, O fair-faced one,
one should again recite the mantra mentally and hold it within the center of the heart. 6.73 One should then hold it from the heart to the pit of the throat, and then between the eyebrows.

Therefore, O best of Brahmins, having mentally ascended the vital breath along with the fire, one whose mind is focused on nothing else should hold it in the ether [of the heart] while uttering the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ),
once the body— with its primary and secondary limbs— has been filled with air within that ether.
Then his self shines there like the sun in the sky,
if he, desiring to cast off the body, practices correctly in this manner,
meditating on the single-syllabled supreme Brahman, the Lord Praṇava.
Having pierced the aperture of Brahmā at the crown of the head with the mind and the vital wind, one should thereafter release the breath into the Great Breath— the void within the center of space,
which transcends the body, is the life-force of the universe, and is the eternal, constant state of emptiness.
6.78ab One should indeed unite one's own self with the supreme bliss in the ether through the intellect;
6.78cd O Gārgī, such a person becomes Brahman itself and shall not undergo birth again.
6.79ab Therefore, O beautiful woman, you too should constantly perform your prescribed duties.
6.79cd Or always perform the restraint of the vital breaths during the periods of the twilights. 6.80ab All those who are devoted to breath control and dedicated to breath control,
6.80cd those who are purified by breath control, attain the supreme goal.
6.81ab There is nothing other than breath control (prāṇāyāma) that delivers one even from hell;
6.81cd for those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, the restraint of the vital breath is the deliverer.
6.82ab Therefore, you should always perform your duties according to the path of the prescribed rules.
6.82cd: "Perform the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇasaṃyamana) according to the path prescribed by the rules.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Śrī Yogayājñavalkya*.

who has the letter *A* as her form, whose limbs are red, who rides upon a swan,

Yājñavalkya said:
"O best of the twice-born, these four limbs of yoga have been described;
now hear the four internal ones, beginning with withdrawal (pratyāhāra)."
7.2ab When the senses wander among their objects by their very nature,
7.2cd the forceful withdrawal of them is called *pratyāhāra*.
7.3ab Whatever you see, all that one should perceive within oneself as being like the Self.

7.4cd their performance within the self by means of the mind, without external [instruments], is [the practice].

7.5cd This withdrawal is praised, as it is always practiced by yogins.
