7.6cd Withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) is said to be the drawing [of the senses] back from each respective location.
7.7ab And likewise, O Gārgī, let the Aśvins, the two best of divine physicians, speak.
7.7cd [They shall describe] the vital points (*marmasthāna*) in the body for the sake of success in yoga and liberation (*yogamokṣa*).
7.8ab I shall describe all of them correctly; listen, O lady of virtuous vows.
7.8cd The two big toes, the two ankles, and likewise the middle of the calves;
7.9ab The root of the buttocks, the two knees, and the middle of the two thighs.
7.9cd Then behind the root of the anus is the middle of the body and the penis;
7.10ab O Gārgī, [then] the navel, the heart, and likewise the pit of the throat;
7.10cd the root of the palate, the root of the nose, and the two circles of the eyes (or, according to VS: the center of the eyes).
7.11ab O best of sages, the space between the eyebrows, the forehead, and the crown of the head—these are the vital points (*marmasthāna*). Listen now to their measurements individually.
7.12ab The measurement from the feet to the ankle is four and a half finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
7.12cd The middle of the calf should be known as being ten finger-breadths from the ankle.
7.13ab From the middle of the calf to the base of the thighs is eleven finger-breadths. 7.13cd From the base of the thighs, O lady of beautiful hips, the knee should be two finger-breadths.
7.14ab The lords of sages say that the middle of the thighs is nine finger-breadths above the knees.
7.14cd Likewise, O Gārgī, the root of the anus is nine finger-breadths from the middle of the thighs.
7.15ab Similarly, the middle of the body is one and a half finger-breadths from the root of the anus.
7.15cd Likewise, from the middle of the body to the penis is two and a half finger-breadths.
7.16ab From the penis, O Gārgī, the navel should be known to be ten and a half finger-breadths away.
7.16cd And from the navel, O fair-faced one, the center of the heart is fourteen finger-breadths.
7.17ab Six finger-breadths from the center of the heart, the pit of the throat is likewise [six finger-breadths].
7.17cd And from the pit of the throat, the root of the tongue is four finger-breadths. 7.18ab The root of the nose is four finger-breadths from the root of the tongue.
7.18cd The location of the eyes is held to be half a finger-breadth from that base.
7.19ab Know that the distance between one's own eyebrows is half a finger-breadth.
7.19cd That which is called the forehead should be two finger-breadths above the midpoint of the eyebrows.
7.20ab From the forehead, that which is known as space extends for exactly three finger-breadths.
7.20cd Having mentally ascended the vital air (vāyu) into these locations, one should hold it there.
7.21ab For one who performs withdrawal (pratyāhāra), drawing [the breath] evenly from each location to the next.

7.21cd All diseases perish and his yogas indeed become perfected. 7.22ab Some men who are skilled in yogas say this, O lady of noble limbs; listen as I describe pratyāhāra to you. 7.22cd Listen, O beautiful one, I shall speak of that.

7.23ab Like a full jar, one should hold the wind from the thumbs to the middle of the head; 7.23cd impelled by breath-control (prāṇāyāma), one should hold the vital air with the intellect and the mind. 7.24ab Having drawn it back through the aperture of space, one should hold it again at the forehead.
7.24cd Drawing the wind from the forehead, one should restrain it between the eyebrows.
7.25ab Drawing [the wind] evenly from between the eyebrows, one should restrain it in the middle of the eyes.
7.25cd Drawing the vital breath (prāṇa) from the eyes, one should restrain it at the root of the nose.
7.26ab One should restrain the vital breath (*prāṇa*) from the base of the nose at the root of the tongue.
7.26cd Having drawn it up from the root of the tongue, one should restrain it at the base of the throat (*kaṇṭhakūpa*).
7.27ab From the base of the throat, however, [one should restrain it] in the middle of the heart; from the heart, into the middle of the navel.

7.27cd Again from the center of the navel to the penis, and from the penis to the abode of fire (the heart); 7.28ab From the middle of the body to the anus, O Gārgī, and from the anus to the base of the thighs;
7.28cd From the base of the thighs to the middle between them, and from there one should restrain [the breath] at the knees.
7.29ab Then, from that root of the fire-altar, likewise from the middle of the shanks;
7.29cd having drawn the wind equally from the middle of the shanks, one should restrain it at the ankle.
7.30ab From the ankle to the two big toes, O Gārgī, one should restrain it in the feet.
7.30cd But the wise person who, having drawn [the breath] from station to station, should thus retain it;
7.31ab With his soul purified of all sins, he shall live as long as the moon and stars endure. 7.31cd This has indeed been proclaimed by Agastya for the sake of attaining perfection in yoga.
7.32ab This is praised by yogis as the best among all types of pratyāhāra.
7.32cd Having filled the breath through both nostrils, one should cast it into the two sides of the *kuṇḍalī*.
7.33ab One should hold it there simultaneously; by that, one is liberated from the disease of worldly existence (*bhava*).
7.33cd Or, having mounted the vital air as before, one should hold it within the space of the heart.
7.34ab O lady of excellent hips, that man also goes to the station of the Supreme Self; 7.34cd how much more so, then, will his diseases—whether existing externally or internally—be destroyed?
Having drawn the breath through both nostrils and filled it within the abdomen,
and having fixed the gaze between the eyebrows and behind the eyes with a concentrated mind,
if one holds it for even a moment, he too attains the supreme goal.
7.36cd What more need be said? Constantly performing one's obligatory duties,
7.37ab and having placed one's own vital breath between the eyebrows by means of the *suṣumnā*,
7.37cd maintain restraint for as long as the mind remains dissolved therein.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Śrī-Yoga-Yājñavalkya.
Yājñavalkya said:
Now, therefore, I shall explain the five types of concentration (dhāraṇā) according to their true nature.

8.1cd Listen with a concentrated mind, O Gārgī, you whose wealth is asceticism. 8.2ab The stabilization of the mind— endowed with qualities such as self-restraint (yama)— within the Self, 8.2cd is called "dhāraṇā" by the virtuous who know the essential purport of the scriptures.
8.3ab O Gārgī, in this city of Brahman, which is this lotus of the heart; 8.3cd within that very space is the support of the external ether.
8.4ab And this is called "dhāraṇā" by those expert in the Yoga scriptures.

8.4cd By the learned tantrikas, experts in the Yoga scriptures, and those well-trained, 8.5ab five types of dhāraṇās have been taught; listen now to all of them individually: 8.5cd Earth, water, fire, air, and space.
8.6ab In these [five locations], the retention of the five deities is said to be fivefold.
8.6cd The region from the feet up to the knees is called the station of earth (pṛthivī). 8.7ab The region from the knees up to the anus is proclaimed as the station of water (ap).
8.7cd That which extends from the anus to the heart is called the locus of fire (vahni). 8.8ab From the middle of the heart up to the middle of the eyebrows is known as the family of wind (vāyu).
8.8cd From the middle of the eyebrows up to the crown of the head is called space (ākāśa).
8.9ab Here, others who consider themselves experts in yoga say:
8.9cd "O twice-born ones, the region from the knees up to the navel is the abode of water.
8.10ab "That which extends from the middle of the navel to the throat is said to be the abode of fire."
8.10cd The region from the throat to the forehead is declared to be the locus of wind (vāyu).
8.11ab The region from the forehead to the cranial aperture is said to be the locus of space (ākāśa).
8.11cd This has been stated by those who know the essential intent of the scriptures to be incorrect.
8.12ab If there were a place for fire within the body, O fair-faced one,
8.12cd it would be illogical for the effect to reside within its cause, which is fire.
8.13ab When the effect and the cause are in conjunction, how could there be a destruction of the effect?
8.13cd This is observed in the forms of their effects, such as jars and the like which consist of clay.
8.14ab O Gārgī, one should place Brahmā Parameṣṭhin upon the earth; Viṣṇu in the waters; Rudra in the fire; and Īśvara in the sphere of wind.
8.15ab One who is well-composed should likewise hold Sadāśiva in the ether (vyoman).
8.15cd Having established the wind upon the earth, conjoined with the syllable *la*,
8.16ab one should meditate on Brahmā, the cause of creation, in his four-armed form.
One should retain [the breath] for five *ghaṭikās* and attain mastery over the earth element.
Having mounted the wind upon the *vāruṇa* [element] and joined it with the syllable *va*,
one should meditate upon the gentle Nārāyaṇa, four-armed and wearing a crown.
8.18ab One who meditates upon Acyuta, who resembles pure crystal and is clad in yellow garments,
for five *ghaṭikās*, is liberated from all diseases. 8.19ab Having established the wind (*anila*) in the fire (*vahni*), [one should place it] together with the syllable *ra* (*repha*).

8.19cd Meditating upon the three-eyed Rudra, the granter of boons, who resembles the rising sun; 8.20ab Whose entire body is smeared with ashes and who is exceedingly gracious— one who maintains this [meditation] for five *ghaṭikās* is not burned by fire.
8.21ab One should hold the wind-element in the station of the wind, conjoined with the letter *ya*, for five *ghaṭikās*. 8.21cd Like the wind, one becomes a traveler in the sky.
8.22ab Having mounted the wind upon space, [one places] the letter *śa* above the letter *ha*.
Mahādeva, whose form is the *bindu*, is Sadāśiva, whose nature is space;
he resembles pure crystal, wears the crescent moon upon his crest,
possesses five faces, is gentle, has ten arms, and three eyes.
8.24ab With hands raised holding all weapons, adorned with all ornaments,
8.24cd having Umā as half of his body, the giver of boons, the cause of all causes—
8.25ab whoever should contemplate him in their mind and hold that [image] even for a moment.
8.25cd He alone is called "liberated" by those well-trained in the Tantras.

8.26ab This is what is meant: O Gārgī, best among the knowers of Brahman, when [the soul] has withdrawn the effects, beginning with Brahmā, each into its own respective cause; 8.26cd [and remains there].
8.27ab Having drawn the vital breath and the mind into that Sadāśiva, the causal source,
8.27cd one whose mind is disciplined should then unite the self with the Supreme Lord.
8.28ab Regarding this matter, other yogins who are the best among the knowers of Brahman say:

8.28cd Having withdrawn all effects into their respective causes by means of the *praṇava* alone, 8.29ab [one should meditate] upon that which consists of the form of supreme bliss at the end of the resonance (*nāda*) of the *praṇava*:
8.29cd The Truth, the Reality, the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣa who is dark and tawny.
The wise perceive with their minds the remedy for saṃsāra.
Therefore, by means of the *praṇava* alone, through three successive breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*),
you should dissolve the effects, beginning with Brahmā, each into its own respective cause.
8.31cd Behold the Supreme Lord at the end of the sound with a purified mind.
8.32ab On this matter, other yogins, the best among the knowers of Brahman, speak thus;
8.32cd O lady of excellent limbs, they are the foremost of physicians, fully established in yogic practices.

8.33ab Thus, the body indeed consists of the five elements; 8.33cd and this very body, O beautiful lady, is composed of wind, bile, and phlegm. 8.34ab For all those whose nature is dominated by wind, who are devoted to the practice of yoga—
8.34cd By the very restraint of the vital breaths (prāṇa), the body undergoes desiccation.

8.35ab However, for those whose constitution is dominated by bile (pitta), the body does not wither quickly. 8.35cd And for those whose constitution is dominated by phlegm (kapha), the body remains full and robust for a long time.
8.36ab However, for one performing *dhāraṇā* on fire, all diseases born of wind (*vāta*) perish.
8.36cd For one always performing *dhāraṇā* on the earth-element (*pārthivāṃśa*) and the water-element (*jalāṃśa*),
8.37ab diseases born of phlegm (*śleṣman*) and those born of wind likewise perish before long.

8.37cd For one who constantly performs concentration (*dhāraṇā*) on the portion of space and the portion of wind, 8.38ab diseases born of the three humors (*tridoṣa*) perish; of this there is no doubt. 8.38cd Regarding this matter, the two Aśvins, the best of physicians, spoke thus.
8.39ab By the very restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa), there is the pacification of the three humors (tridoṣa) for men.
8.39cd Therefore, O lady of excellent hips, you too should constantly perform this practice.
8.40ab Endowed with the restraints (yama) and other disciplines, perform concentration (dhāraṇā) according to the prescribed rule.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Śrī Yogayājñavalkya.
Yājñavalkya said:
"Now I shall explain meditation; listen, O Gārgī of lovely countenance."
9.1cd For meditation alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for living beings.
9.2ab Meditation is indeed the perception of the nature of the Self by means of the mind.
9.2cd And that is both with attributes (saguṇa) and without attributes (nirguṇa); it is traditionally taught that the qualified form is manifold.
9.3ab Among those, the best of the twice-born say that five are the most excellent according to the Vedic tradition;

9.3cd three of these are the most principal, while one indeed is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa). 9.4ab [They describe] the vital points (marmasthāna) of the channels (nāḍī) and their respective locations individually.
9.4cd Having understood the locations and functions of the vital airs (vāyu), perform the realization of the Self.
9.5ab [The Self is] one, consisting of light, pure, all-pervading, firm like space, 9.5cd unmanifest, immovable, eternal, and devoid of beginning, middle, or end.
9.6ab It is gross, subtle, formless, intangible, and invisible;
9.6cd it has no taste and is not called fragrance; it is immeasurable and incomparable.
9.7ab It is bliss, undecaying, eternal, both being and non-being, and the cause of all.
9.7cd The support of all, having the form of the world, formless, unborn, and imperishable;
9.8ab Invisible and visible, situated within and situated without, facing in every direction;
9.8cd All-seeing, with feet everywhere, touching everything, with heads on all sides.
9.9ab: "May I be Brahman, composed of Brahman"—whatever realization of this may arise, 9.9cd: that is known by the knowers of Brahman as this meditation (dhyāna) devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
9.10ab: Or else, [the meditation upon] the Supreme Self, whose form is supreme bliss...
9.10cd Having understood the person who is dark and tawny through the instruction of the Guru, 9.11ab and [having realized] Brahman in this city of Brahman, in the center of the small lotus,
9.11cd the virtuous perceive, through practice, that which is the medicine for the cycle of existence.
9.12ab Within the heart-lotus, which possesses eight petals and has arisen from the center of the *kanda*,
9.12cd and whose stalk is twelve finger-breadths long with its face turned upward four finger-breadths—
9.13ab when this [lotus] has blossomed through breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), it is endowed with filaments and a pericarp.
Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, Nārāyaṇa, the unborn Hari—
four-armed, with noble limbs, bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
wearing a crown and armlets, with eyes like lotus petals.

9.15ab Viṣṇu, whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark, whose face resembles the full moon; 9.15cd whose lips have the luster of the interior petals of a lotus, who is most serene and possesses a pure smile;
9.16ab who resembles pure crystal, who is clad in yellow garments, and is the infallible Acyuta.

Having mentally beheld the Lord of Gods, who dwells in the hearts of all beings— the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), the imperishable Supreme Self, whose form is illuminated on all sides by splendors, and whose pair of lotus-hued feet [shine forth]— 9.16cd–9.17ab.

9.18ab This cognition, "I am that Self," is called meditation with attributes (saguṇa-dhyāna). 9.18cd It is within the lotus of the heart, whose pericarp consists of primordial nature (prakṛti), 9.19ab which is endowed with the eight petals of sovereign powers (aiśvarya) and possessed of the filaments of knowledge (vidyā).
Upon the stalk of knowledge, rooted in the great bulb (kanda) and awakened by breath control (prāṇāyāma),
[one perceives] the Vaiśvānara, the Lord, the source of the universe, whose body is a crest of flame, a great fire blazing with universal radiance and facing in all directions.

9.21ab Seeing his own body heated from the soles of the feet to the head, 9.21cd and the blazing fire within it like a lamp in a windless place, 9.22ab he beheld the imperishable Supreme Self in the midst of its flames.
9.22cd Resplendent like a streak of lightning in the midst of dark blue clouds;
9.23ab Having known the god Vaiśvānara, whose form is like the awn of wild rice (nīvāra) and has a yellowish luster, as the cause of all— 9.23cd The realization that "I am He" is the [true] Self.
9.24ab For those who know yoga, they recognize this meditation as the highest among those with attributes (saguṇa).
9.24cd Having attained the state of Vaiśvānara, one goes to liberation by that very means. 9.25ab Alternatively, one should behold the orb of the sun of great splendor.
9.25cd [He saw] himself as the Puruṣa of the entire world, having the form of gold;
9.26ab Hari, with golden beard and hair, and golden nails; 9.26cd his face like that of a monkey, the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction.
Seated in the lotus posture, gentle, with a face like a blossoming lotus,
his eyes possessing the luster of the interior petals of a lotus, he brings fear to all the worlds;
he knows everything at all times and elevates those who follow the Dharma.
9.28cd Having seen him who illuminates the entire world, the sole witness of the universe;
9.29ab the realization "I am he" is that which is praised in meditations.
9.29cd This alone, O lady rich in austerity, is the great path to liberation.
9.30ab By means of this solar meditation, the wise attain liberation.
9.30cd [They meditate on] the inner self between the eyebrows, whose form is light and who is the cause of all.
9.31ab Like a pillar, it has arisen from the middle of the body and extends up to the crown of the head.
9.31cd Having perceived with the mind the unmanifest cause of the world, blazing and of immeasurable splendor, [thinking] "May I become that"— this is the supreme meditation.
9.32ab Alternatively, while seated in the bound lotus posture with the body relaxed...

9.33ab Having himself become Śiva, with his gaze fixed upon the tip of the nose, 9.33cd he should meditate, O fair-faced one, upon the Supreme Lord, the Self, who is changeless, supremely peaceful, 9.34ab consisting of light, immortal, and situated between the eyebrows.
9.34cd That cognition which [perceives] "I am indeed that" is praised in the meditations (dhyāna).
9.35ab Alternatively, within the blooming lotus of the heart, endowed with eight petals, possessed of a pericarp and filaments, and situated in the center of the lunar orb; 9.35cd [therein...]
9.36ab One’s own self, appearing in the form of a child, is the imperishable enjoyer;
9.36cd it is enveloped by the rays of the moon that discharge the essence of nectar.
9.37ab [It is situated] from the downward-facing lotus of the head, which is endowed with sixteen petals.
Having meditated with a concentrated mind upon that person there being bathed on all sides by thousands of streams of nectar flowing forth,
[he should contemplate] that very body, including its limbs and minor members, with that essence of nectar.
9.39ab I alone am the supreme Brahman; I am the immutable Supreme Self. 9.39cd Such knowledge as this is called meditation with attributes (saguṇa-dhyāna).
9.40ab By thus partaking of the nectar of meditation for six months, one becomes a conqueror of death.
9.40cd He shall indeed be liberated for years while still living; of this there is no doubt.
9.41ab For one who is liberated while living, there is no attainment of suffering whatsoever in any way.
9.41cd How much more so for one eternally liberated—for such a one, liberation itself is difficult to attain [as a further goal].
Therefore, O lady of excellent hips, you too, having forever renounced the fruits [of action],
should always practice meditation alone while performing your duties according to the prescribed rules. The best of sages have also spoken of many other forms of meditation.
9.43cd These have been declared as the primary means; the others, however, are secondary.
9.44ab Having discerned within oneself whether one possesses qualities or is devoid of them, 9.44cd the virtuous practice meditative absorption (samādhi); you too should always do likewise.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the glorious *Yogayājñavalkya*.
Yājñavalkya said:
10.1ab Now I shall describe *samādhi*, which destroys the bonds of worldly existence.
10.1cd You ought to hear correctly [the teaching] for one who is bound by the fetters of existence.
10.2ab Samādhi is the state of equality between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman).
10.2cd That which is the abiding in Brahman alone is the samādhi of the inner self (pratyagātman).
10.3ab To the extent that one meditates upon the self, to that same extent is there absorption (*samādhi*).
10.3cd Having meditated, the self must be established within the self; otherwise, the self will not become as it should. (VS 4.60 = *dhyānenātmani saṃsthāpya...*)
10.4ab In this very same way, whatever a man has taken refuge in everywhere, 10.4cd he becomes of that very nature and attains meditative absorption (samādhi) therein.
10.5ab Just as water poured into the lord of rivers follows it without distinction, [so does the mind follow its object].
10.5cd Thus, indeed, being non-different from the Self, one should attain meditative absorption (samādhi) here.
10.6ab This is what is meant here, O Gārgī, best among the knowers of Brahman:
10.6cd While performing ritual action according to the rules, one should be free from desire and mental construction (saṃkalpa).
10.7–8. O fair-faced one, one whose mind is always well-trained in the Vedāntas and the Śāstras, having been instructed by the Guru in the meaning endowed with logical reasoning,
and having deliberated again and again with learned men who know the Dharmaśāstras—

10.8cd–10.9ab: With a mind always well-trained in those matters that are firmly determined, one should constantly practice yoga alone regarding the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman). 10.9cd:
Then, by means of internal signs or external indicators of time, [one should recognize the appropriate moments].
10.10 Having determined the time for himself, or [having been prompted] by others, the knower of the ultimate truth—
fearless, with a perfectly serene mind, a mortal who has conquered his senses,
devoted to his own duty, tranquil, and intent on the welfare of all beings— [should depart].

10.11cd Having bestowed the knowledge and the mantra upon his son according to the prescribed rites, 10.12ab and having then instructed him in all the purificatory ceremonies for himself, O sinless one,
10.12cd [he did so] in a sacred field, in a pure place, surrounded by the learned.
10.13ab Having spread kuśa grass upon the ground, or else a black antelope skin, 10.13cd upon that [seat], with his cross-legged posture firmly established and his body bound by mantras,
10.14ab he sits on the seat with undistracted mind, facing either eastward or northward.

10.14cd Having restrained the nine gates within this city of Brahman, O Gārgī, 10.15ab when the lotus of the heart has been awakened by breath-control (prāṇāyāma), [one perceives] in that sky which is the nature of light, one's own true nature, the cause of all.
10.15cd [In that] space which is of the form of radiance, the essential self, the cause of everything.
10.16ab Having thoroughly restrained the activity of the mind within the Supreme Self, the wise man,
10.16cd having placed his own vital breath in the crown of the head or else between the eyebrows, 10.17ab remains established in the cause that is supreme bliss, performing the concentration of yoga.
10.17cd Uttering with his intellect the single syllable "Om," being well-composed,
10.18ab the wise man, that best of men, should cast off the body and become the Self itself;
10.18cd in which [the syllable] the wise man should practice the vision of the Self through yoga alone.

10.19ab Remembering that very [state], the wise man should cast off the body at the end. 10.19cd Whatever state he remembers clearly when he casts off the body at the end, 10.20ab to that very state he goes; thus the knowers of yoga understand.
10.20cd And you too, having established yourself in yoga, meditate upon your own self within the Self.
10.21ab Devoted to their own duty and tranquil, they cast off their bodies at the end. 10.21cd This occurs for one who performs obligatory duties together with this very knowledge.
10.22ab For one who has desisted from attachment to the fruits [of action], O Gārgī, liberation rests in the palm of the hand.
10.22cd That which was previously stated by Brahmā regarding the conjunction of karma and yoga— 10.23ab all that has now been proclaimed according to rule, together with its limbs and sub-limbs.
10.23cd And you too, having practiced yoga endowed with the eight limbs beginning with *yama*,
10.24ab and having attained the state beyond description (*nirvārṇa*), completely renounce the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the *Śrī-Yogayājñavalkya*.
11.1ab Thus addressed by the wise sage Yājñavalkya, 11.1cd the woman of beautiful form spoke these words in the midst of the seers.
Gārgī said:
"O Lord, how may a man devoted to yoga perform his prescribed duties at the two twilights or always? And what is the expiation for one who does not perform them?
Having been addressed thus by the woman who speaks of Brahman, the Brāhmaṇa who knows Brahman then replied:
11.3cd Having observed her, the Blessed One, the best of men, spoke this.
Yājñavalkya said:
11.4ab "For a person engaged in yoga, [this occurs] at the two twilights or even at night."
11.4cd Whatever is to be performed, O beautiful lady, has indeed been accomplished through yoga.
11.5ab When the fire of the self’s *agnihotra* has been intensified by means of breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*),
11.5cd for one who offers the prescribed ritual action as an oblation with the clarified butter of a purified mind.
11.6ab What atonement can there be for that, O fool? For he is indeed then one who has accomplished his purpose (kṛtakṛtya).
11.6cd This is when the separation between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) has been attained.
11.7ab Those who know Brahman must constantly perform the actions prescribed by the injunctions.
11.7cd And if a yogin should abandon [action] thinking only "it is suffering" at the time of separation [from the body],
11.8ab hell is proclaimed to be his abode. 11.8cd For it is not possible for embodied beings to abandon actions entirely.
11.9ab Therefore, until death, yogis should always perform the prescribed rite. 11.9cd You too, O Gārgī, must not neglect; perform the prescribed action without delay. (Do not abandon it.)
"By means of yoga, worship the Supreme Self and abandon the body.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Yājñavalkya, a treasure-house of austerity,
looked toward the sages with his eyes and addressed these words to them.
"Having performed the evening twilight rites according to the rules with well-concentrated minds,
let all you sages now depart for your own hermitages. Thus addressed by the sage, the sages who were devoted to their vows [prepared to leave].
Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, and likewise Aṅgiras;
Agastya, Nārada, Vālmīki, and Bādarāyaṇi; Paiṅgi, Dīrghatamas, Vyāsa, and Śaunaka, whose wealth is asceticism.
Bhārgava, Kāśyapa, and likewise Bharadvāja,
as well as other ascetics who were knowers of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
having honored Yājñavalkya with excellent words and blessings, [spoke].
11.16ab All those sages departed for their own hermitages just as they had come.
11.16cd When these ascetics, whose wealth was their austerity, had gone to their own hermitages, [Rāma], having prostrated himself on the ground like a staff, spoke these words:
11.17ab [He] addressed this speech after bowing down upon the earth like a staff.
Gārgya said: "O Blessed One, knower of all scriptures, devoted to the welfare of all beings,
O Lord of Yogins, that which has been spoken by you for the sake of liberation from worldly existence— "
11.18cd Yoga, accompanied by the eight limbs beginning with restraint (yama), is indeed the means to liberation.
11.19ab All of this has been forgotten in your presence, O Omniscient One.
11.19cd Therefore, please instruct me today in yoga, together with its limbs, in a concise form.
"O Omniscient One, you ought to rescue me from the ocean of birth and saṃsāra.
Thus addressed by the woman who spoke of Brahman, that Brāhmaṇa, a knower of Brahman,
then looked upon her in pity and spoke with a smile.
11.21cd Arise, arise! Why do you lie on the ground, O Gārgī of lovely countenance?
11.22ab I shall explain to you in brief the yoga; listen now to it.
11.22cd Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Śrī-Yogayājñavalkya.
Yājñavalkya said:
Pressing the anus with the left ankle and pressing the joint with the other [ankle],
placing the right hand on the left [knee], gaze at the flame of the fire.
12.2ab When the prāṇa, which causes the destruction of life,
is indeed restrained by means of the āsana, Gārgī, it then proceeds very slowly from that [prāṇa] into the apāna.
12.3ab The fire, fanned by the wind of the apāna, moves very slowly.
12.3cd Then it blazes within the bodies of all those in one's own lineage. 12.4ab Being composed, one should practice thus at dawn, at twilight, and at midnight.
12.4cd One should practice for a muhūrta in this manner for as long as two five-day periods.
12.5ab Then, O best of Brahmins, various signs of success arise individually within his own self;
at that time, he by whom the vital breath (samīraṇa) has been conquered [is known].
12.6ab Lightness of the body and the radiance of the fire residing in the stomach [occur].
12.6cd Indeed, these signs first appear as the manifestation of the sound (*nāda*).
12.7ab One’s urine and feces become scanty after six months or even a year. 12.7cd Later, while sitting or riding, one should not fear [an accident] for three years.
(V.S. 4.16) "He cannot be pierced by others, whether from his seat or his vehicle.

12.8ab: Then, having placed the wind together with the breath-pleasure within the intellect, one should restrain it. 12.8cd: Constantly meditating upon the Discus-bearer, who is unawakened and always situated in the *kuṇḍalinī* at the navel.
12.9ab Having encircled the central channel with her mouth, and likewise the other channels with her body;
12.9cd Having properly grasped her own tail with her mouth and restrained the paths of the hosts of winds;
12.10ab Ever awakened, breathing like a sleeping lord of serpents, she blazes with splendor.
12.10cd That Kuṇḍalinī always resides at the navel; likewise, she exists in other bodies in a transverse position.

12.11ab With the flames of fire fanned by the vital air, he who—by means of the channels situated within the *kanda*— 12.11cd burns the Kuṇḍalinī, which has the form of an outer coil, while meditating upon her, is indeed that best of men.
12.12ab Scorched there by fire and agitated by the wind,

12.12cd that [serpent] then awakens, extending the coils of its hood. 12.13ab When the Wielder of the Discus has attained awakening in the center of the navel, the vital breaths gather together in this Kavalīra.
12.13cd All move together with the fire alone, just as the movement of threads occurs within a cloth.
12.14ab Having thus conquered the station of the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu), being ever devoted to meditation,
12.14cd one should then lead the *apāna* upward from the navel, while recollecting this.
Just as the wind, together with the friend of wind (fire), having passed through the body, [the winds] depart;
then diseases perish, strength increases, and a radiant luster arises when [the breath] has awakened.
Here, the winds, together with fire, go forth, gathering [the vital energies] toward the opening of the *brahmarandhra*.

12.16cd By some means here, I shall tell you: through the sight of the beautiful flame of the lamp within the heart, 12.17ab the wind in the heart is restrained by that [means]. When, together with the friend of the wind (fire), 12.17cd having entered the mouth of the thousand-petaled lotus, the double-tongued one (the serpent) makes it face upward once again.
12.18ab O Gārgya, when the lotus of the heart has blossomed in this city of Brahman,
12.18cd the wind shines like a row of young suns in the sky.
12.19ab At that time, the consumer of oblations (the fire) is situated within the *suṣumṇā* from the center of the heart.
12.19cd Like a streak of lightning amidst banks of water-laden clouds, [it] shines.
12.20ab When the fire is established within the awakened lotus of the heart and the vital breath (prāṇa) is likewise placed therein,
12.20cd external and internal signs, visible like a lamp and so forth, arise for him.
12.21ab Then, uttering the *praṇava* together with the *bindu*, one should draw up the wind along with fire.
12.21cd With the intellect, one should contemplate the crescent moon upon the forehead, which resembles a young moon.
12.22ab Having then mentally mounted the wind along with fire between the eyebrows, one should proceed.
12.22cd Then, with undistracted mind, one should meditate upon the inner self within.
12.23ab Even in the navel, the heart, and the forehead, the invisible mark blazes like a pillar.
12.23cd O Gārgī, this is the ultimate reality; behold it, behold it with the mind as a beautiful form.
12.24ab He who perceives the radiance consisting of knowledge in the center of the forehead and in the lotus of the heart,
12.24cd that knower of Brahman always sees the Śakti blazing like a lamp with a single gaze. 12.25ab When the mind of yogis and men attains dissolution in the space between the eyebrows...
(For yogins, between the eyebrows...
12.25cd: At the root of the tongue there is the flow of nectar, and between the eyebrows there is the vision of the Self.
12.26ab: Likewise, there is trembling of the head, and the vision of the Self by means of the mind alone.

The delightful celestial gardens, the stars, and the moon, as well as the ṛṣis, siddhas, and gandharvas, become manifest to yogins. When the mind reaches dissolution in the light within the space between the eyebrows at the station of Viṣṇu, it becomes awakened.
12.27cd Having practiced thus for some time, again meditate happily upon the full form in the midst of space.
12.28ab When the breath has settled in the station of Viṣṇu (the *viṣṇupada*), and when the individual soul (*jīva*) is merged in that nectar;
12.28cd then the mind attains dissolution therein; they say that this is close to liberation.

12.29 When the vital breath has entered Viṣṇupada and the intellect is purified, being then established in the Self, there is indeed a most wonderful bliss; O Gārgī, behold it today with a purified intellect.
12.30 Having thus practiced for a very long time, with the body disciplined by the restraints (yama) and other means, and eating in moderation—

12.30cd Having reached the Self that has entered the cave, attain liberation once more in the city of Brahman. 12.31ab O Gārgī, from whom all beings arise, by whom the moving and unmoving creatures live, and into whom, once born, they go to their dissolution—know that to be Brahman; so say all.
12.32ab That which is of a single form within the lotus of the heart, in the void—eternal, consisting of bliss, and extremely subtle;

12.32cd that Brahman, consisting of light, [resides] in the cave, so the Śruti declares. 12.33ab Smaller than the smallest and greater than the greatest, the Self is hidden in the cave of this living being.
12.33cd Behold him who is devoid of ritual action with a purified intellect, and at the time of departure, be free from sorrow.
12.34ab Having reached the Prabhajana wind located in the head together with fire through the wisdom derived from the teacher’s instruction,
12.34cd pierce the crown of the head and, recollecting the syllable *oṃ*, cast off your vital breaths into the midst of the sky.
12.35ab If, out of desire, you wish to know how to relinquish the body, my friend, I shall tell you.
12.35cd Uttering the *praṇava*, raise it to the crown of your head; having split [the body], join it with that [supreme] self. 12.36ab This is the supreme purifier, yoga endowed with its eight limbs.
12.36cd This most secret and meritorious knowledge has been proclaimed to you, O fair-faced one.
12.37ab That best of men who would constantly hear this narrative concerning yoga,
12.37cd being liberated from all sins, shall become one possessed of perfect knowledge.
12.38ab But the wise man who, constantly endowed with devotion, causes this to be heard,
12.38cd the sin committed in a single lifetime perishes in a single day.
12.39ab Or that man who hears this exposition of yoga even once—

12.39cd All the sin produced by ignorance is destroyed for him. 12.40ab Those who constantly perform their obligatory duties endowed with self-knowledge— 12.40cd seeing them engaged in their daily rites, even the gods bow down to them.
"Therefore, O Gārgī, embodied beings who fear worldly existence must perform obligatory rites according to the rules until the end of the body through knowledge, and they must also practice yoga.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One revealed this secret, which produces liberation, to her.
12.42cd The best of the twice-born sat in solitude in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the nectar of yoga that is the cause for the destruction of bondage.
12.43ab Having honored that sage— who was speaking, who was great, a treasury of knowledge, and the most eminent among the knowers of Brahman—
12.43cd with words and prostrations, she, the most excellent of the virtuous, attained a constant, supreme, and pure joy.
12.44ab Then, having well grasped that yoga which is born of the secret [teachings], which is secret itself, and which brings liberation to living beings,
12.44cd she cast off the cycle of worldly existence and, filled with constant joy, entered a secluded dwelling in the forest.
12.45ab By whom this entire manifold world is filled, and by whom alone the whole universe appears—
12.45cd Beholding that Vāsudeva, who is born at the pinnacle of the Vedas, he always remains with him in his heart and on his head day after day.

12.46ab That which is one, unmanifest, infinite, infallible, the cause of the birth and so forth of the phenomenal world, and immeasurable— 12.46cd Beholding that Vāsudeva, who is born at the pinnacle of the Vedas, he always remains with him in his heart and on his head day after day.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Śrī Yogayājñavalkya;
this treatise on Yoga is complete.
